conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim that influenza vaccination causes Alzheimer's disease is 'false and unsupported by scientific evidence' and highlights studies showing that flu vaccination is actually associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
## Conclusion

The claim that influenza vaccination causes Alzheimer's disease is **false and unsupported by scientific evidence**. Multiple peer-reviewed studies consistently show the opposite: influenza vaccination is associated with a **reduced**, not increased, risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia.

A large retrospective cohort study of nearly 2 million adults found that flu-vaccinated individuals aged 65+ had roughly a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease compared with unvaccinated peers (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9484126/). A more recent study comparing high-dose versus standard-dose flu vaccines in nearly 200,000 older adults found the high-dose vaccine was associated with a further reduction in Alzheimer's dementia risk—more pronounced in women (https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000214782). A broader analysis in *Age and Ageing* similarly found that adult vaccinations, including influenza, herpes zoster, pneumococcal, and Tdap vaccines, are associated with lower dementia risk (https://academic.oup.com/ageing/article/54/11/afaf331/8339764).

The origin of the "flu shot causes Alzheimer's" claim traces to unsubstantiated remarks by Hugh Fudenberg, a discredited immunologist whose assertions were never published in peer-reviewed literature and have been debunked by fact-checkers, including Snopes (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/flu-shot-avoidance/) and Science-Based Medicine. No credible scientific body supports a causal link between influenza vaccination and Alzheimer's disease.

**Bottom line:** Current evidence indicates influenza vaccination does not cause Alzheimer's disease; if anything, it appears to be associated with a protective effect against dementia, likely due to prevention of infection-related inflammation and reduced severe illness in older adults.
